tips.title: Normal to the surface, per unit area
tips.body: $p = \dfrac{F}{A}$, where the force acts at **right angles** to the surface. It is not on the equation sheet, so learn it. A pascal is one newton per square metre.

tips.title: Convert the area to square metres
tips.body: An area in cm² must be divided by 10 000 to become m², not by 100. Getting this wrong changes the answer by a factor of ten thousand, which is the biggest single error in the topic.

tips.title: Depth, density, gravity
tips.body: $p = h\rho g$ says pressure in a liquid depends on the **depth**, the **density** and gravity, and not at all on the shape of the container or the area of the base.

tips.title: Square metres, straight away
tips.body: Convert any area to **square metres** before dividing, remembering that $1$ m² is $10\,000$ cm², not 100. Doing it in the first line keeps the answer in pascals, and it is a far commoner source of lost marks than the physics itself.

steps.title: Pressure: how concentrated a force is
steps.body:
Push on a wall with your palm and nothing happens. Push with the same force through a drawing pin and it goes in. The force is the same; what changed is the **area** it acts on.

$$p = \dfrac{F}{A}$$

$p$ is pressure in pascals (Pa), $F$ is force in newtons, $A$ is area in square metres. One pascal is one newton spread over one square metre, so Pa and N/m² mean the same thing.

This equation is **not on the equation sheet**. You have to know it.

visuals.alt: A card showing pressure equals force divided by area, with units pascals, newtons and square metres

check.prompt: A force of 30 N acts on an area of 3 m². Calculate the pressure.

steps.title: Small area, big pressure
steps.body:
Halve the area and you double the pressure. That one idea explains a lot of everyday design:

- Knives, needles and drawing pins have tiny areas so a small force makes a huge pressure.
- Snowshoes, camel feet and tractor tyres have large areas so a large weight makes a small pressure and does not sink in.

The unit trap: areas in exam questions are often given in cm² or mm². Convert to m² **before** dividing. $1$ m² $= 10\,000$ cm² $= 1\,000\,000$ mm².

visuals.problem: Same 600 N person, two pairs of shoes

steps.text: Flat shoes, total area $0.03$ m²: $p = 600 \div 0.03 = 20\,000$ Pa
Stiletto heels, total area $0.0002$ m²: $p = 600 \div 0.0002 = 3\,000\,000$ Pa
150 times the pressure, from the same weight
steps.note: That is why heels dent floors and an elephant does not

check.prompt: A force of 50 N acts on 25 cm². What is the pressure in pascals?
check.solution: $25$ cm² $= 0.0025$ m². $50 \div 0.0025 = 20\,000$ Pa. Dividing by 25 without converting gives 2 Pa, which is the common wrong answer.
options: 2 Pa
200 Pa

steps.title: Pressure in a fluid pushes every way
steps.body:
A **fluid** is anything that flows: a liquid or a gas. The particles in a fluid move in every direction and collide with every surface they meet, so a fluid pushes on **all** of the surfaces around it, not just the bottom.

The pressure at a point in a fluid causes a force **at right angles** (normal) to any surface at that point. That is why water squirts sideways out of a hole in a bottle, why your ears feel it underwater from every side, and why a submarine's hull has to be strong all the way round.

visuals.alt: A tank of water with pressure arrows pushing sideways on its wall at 1, 2 and 3 metres depth, each arrow longer than the one above

check.prompt: A small hole is made in the side of a tank of water. Which way does the water first move?
check.skill: direction of pressure in a fluid
check.solution: Pressure in a fluid causes a force at right angles to any surface. At the wall, that force pushes the water straight out through the hole.

markScheme.description: out at right angles to the wall

options: Straight downwards
Straight out, at right angles to the wall
Upwards
It stays still, because pressure only acts downwards

steps.title: Deeper means more pressure
steps.body:
Higher tier, Physics only. Stand at the bottom of a swimming pool and the whole column of water above you is pressing down. Go deeper and the column is taller, so it weighs more, so the pressure is greater.

$$p = h \rho g$$

$h$ is depth in m, $\rho$ (rho) is the density of the liquid in kg/m³, $g$ is $9.8$ N/kg. Water is $1000$ kg/m³; sea water about $1030$ kg/m³.

Where it comes from: a column of liquid of height $h$ over an area $A$ has volume $hA$, mass $\rho h A$, and weight $\rho h A g$. Divide that weight by the area $A$ and the $A$ cancels, leaving $h \rho g$.

This one **is** on the equation sheet. Two points to notice: the pressure depends on the **depth**, not the shape or width of the container, and it depends on the **density**, so the same depth in sea water gives a little more pressure than in fresh water.

visuals.alt: A tank of water with pressure arrows at 1, 2 and 3 metres depth, labelled 9.8 kPa, 19.6 kPa and 29.4 kPa, each arrow longer than the one above

visuals.problem: Find the pressure due to the water at the bottom of a 1.5 m deep swimming pool. Density 1000 kg/m³, $g = 9.8$ N/kg. Give the answer in kPa.

steps.note: depth in m, density in kg/m³, $g$ in N/kg
all inputs in SI units, so the answer is in Pa
divide by 1000 for kPa; read which unit the question wants

steps.text: Same depth in sea water: $1.5 \times 1030 \times 9.8 = 15\,141$ Pa, about 15.1 kPa
steps.note: denser liquid, slightly more pressure at the same depth

check.prompt: Calculate the pressure due to water at a depth of 3 m. Density $= 1000$ kg/m³, $g = 9.8$ N/kg.

steps.title: Adding the atmosphere on top
steps.body:
$h \rho g$ gives the pressure caused **by the liquid**. But there is already air pressing on the surface of the liquid, at about $100\,000$ Pa, and that pressure is passed all the way down.

So the **total** pressure at a depth is atmospheric pressure **plus** $h \rho g$. A question that gives you atmospheric pressure and asks for *the total pressure* wants both added; a question that asks for *the pressure due to the water* wants $h \rho g$ on its own. Read which one it is.

visuals.problem: Total pressure on a diver at 20 m in sea water, atmospheric pressure 101 000 Pa

steps.text: Pressure due to the water: $p = h \rho g = 20 \times 1030 \times 9.8 = 201\,880$ Pa
Add the atmosphere on the surface: $201\,880 + 101\,000 = 302\,880$ Pa

steps.note: Every 10 m of water adds roughly one more atmosphere

check.prompt: Atmospheric pressure is 100 000 Pa. What is the total pressure at a depth of 5 m in fresh water? Density $= 1000$ kg/m³, $g = 9.8$ N/kg.

steps.title: Upthrust: why things float
steps.body:
Higher tier, Physics only. Put a block under water. Its bottom face is deeper than its top face, so the pressure on the bottom is greater than the pressure on the top. Same area, more pressure, more force: the push **up** on the bottom beats the push **down** on the top.

The difference is a resultant force upwards called **upthrust**, and it is always equal to the **weight of the fluid the object has pushed out of the way**. A bigger object displaces more fluid and gets more upthrust.

Whether something floats is a straight comparison:

- Upthrust **greater than** weight: it rises. At the surface it settles where it displaces exactly its own weight of fluid, and floats there.
- Upthrust **equal to** weight while fully submerged: it stays where it is, neither rising nor sinking.
- Upthrust **less than** weight: it sinks.

An object **less dense** than the fluid can always displace its own weight, so it floats. Steel is denser than water, but a steel ship is mostly air, so its average density is lower and it floats.

visuals.alt: A block hanging in a tank of water, with a longer arrow pushing up on its bottom face than the arrow pushing down on its top face

check.prompt: A fully submerged object weighs 8 N and the upthrust on it is 8 N. What happens?
check.solution: The two forces are equal and opposite, so the resultant force is zero and the object stays put. It would rise if the upthrust were larger and sink if the weight were.
options: It stays where it is, neither rising nor sinking
It floats with half of it above the water
It shoots up to the surface
It sinks to the bottom

steps.title: The atmosphere is a fluid too
steps.body:
The air around the Earth is a **thin layer of gas** held down by gravity. Like any fluid, it presses on everything inside it, and at sea level that pressure is about $100\,000$ Pa, one atmosphere. You do not feel it because it pushes equally from every side and the air inside you pushes back.

The model AQA wants is simple. Air can be compressed, so gravity pulls the molecules towards the surface and the air is **densest at the bottom** and gets **thinner with height**. Atmospheric pressure at any level is the **weight of the air above** that level.

So pressure falls as you go up, for two reasons at once: there is less air above you, and the air that is there is less dense. At the top of Everest the pressure is about a third of the sea-level value. Aircraft cabins are pressurised for exactly this reason.

visuals.problem: Why the pressure at height is lower

steps.text: At sea level the whole atmosphere is above you: its full weight presses down, about $100\,000$ Pa
At 5 km up, roughly half the air's mass is now below you: only the rest presses down
And the air up there is thinner, so each metre of height adds less weight than a metre near the ground
Less air above, and thinner air: pressure at height is lower
steps.note: Both halves of the reason earn marks; give both

check.prompt: Which of these is the reason atmospheric pressure is about 100 000 Pa at sea level?
check.solution: Atmospheric pressure at any level is caused by the weight of the air above it. At sea level that is the whole atmosphere.

markScheme.description: the weight of the air above

options: Gravity is strongest at sea level
The weight of all the air above sea level presses down on it
The sea pushes up on the air
Air molecules at sea level are heavier than those higher up

steps.title: Your turn: pressure against depth
steps.body:
The slider sets the depth in fresh water. Read off the pressure due to the water.

The graph is a straight line through the origin because $p = h \rho g$ with $\rho g$ fixed: the gradient is $\rho g = 1000 \times 9.8 = 9800$ Pa per metre. Check: at 4 m the pressure should be $39\,200$ Pa.

visuals.fallback: A straight line from the origin with gradient 9800: 19 600 Pa at 2 m, 49 000 Pa at 5 m, 98 000 Pa at 10 m.

check.prompt: Using $p = h \rho g$, what is the pressure due to the water at 8 m depth? Density $= 1000$ kg/m³, $g = 9.8$ N/kg.

steps.title: Going deeper: working out upthrust from pressure
steps.body:
The question that sorts out the top grades asks you to **calculate** the upthrust rather than name it. The route is the one the lesson used to explain it:

1. Pressure on the top face, $h_1 \rho g$.
2. Pressure on the bottom face, $h_2 \rho g$, with $h_2$ deeper.
3. The difference in pressure, times the area of a face, is the upthrust.

The number you get is always the weight of the displaced fluid, so you can check it that way.

The other grade 9 habit is reading exactly what is asked. *Pressure due to the water* is $h \rho g$. *Total pressure* adds the atmosphere. *Increase in pressure* between two depths is $\Delta h \, \rho g$, and the atmosphere cancels because it is the same at both depths.

visuals.alt: A cube hanging in water with its top at 0.2 m and its bottom at 0.3 m, with a longer arrow pushing up than down

visuals.problem: Upthrust on a 0.1 m cube with its top 0.2 m under water

steps.text: Difference: $980$ Pa, on a face of area $0.01$ m²

steps.note: Check: $0.001$ m³ of water weighs $0.001 \times 1000 \times 9.8 = 9.8$ N

check.prompt: A cube of side 0.2 m is submerged with its top face 0.5 m deep. Calculate the upthrust. Density $= 1000$ kg/m³, $g = 9.8$ N/kg.
check.solution: Top: $0.5 \times 9800 = 4900$ Pa. Bottom at $0.7$ m: $6860$ Pa. Difference $1960$ Pa on $0.04$ m²: $78.4$ N. Check: $0.008$ m³ of water weighs $78.4$ N.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Pressure** $p = \dfrac{F}{A}$, in Pa (N/m²). Not on the sheet. Convert cm² to m² before dividing.
- **Fluids push in every direction**, at right angles to any surface.
- **Pressure in a liquid** $p = h \rho g$: depends on depth and density, not the shape of the container. On the sheet.
- **Total pressure** at a depth is atmospheric pressure plus $h \rho g$. Read whether the question wants *total* or *due to the water*.
- **Upthrust** is the bottom face being pushed harder than the top face. It equals the weight of fluid displaced.
- **Floats** if upthrust can reach the weight, which happens when the object is less dense than the fluid. Sinks otherwise.
- **The atmosphere** is a thin layer of gas, densest at the surface. Its pressure is the weight of the air above, so it falls with height.

visuals.alt: A card with the pressure equation, the depth pressure equation, and upthrust as the weight of fluid displaced

questions.prompt: A force of 200 N acts on an area of 4 m². Calculate the pressure.
What is the unit of pressure?
questions.solution: Pressure is force divided by area, newtons per square metre, and 1 N/m² is called 1 pascal (Pa).
options: Pa
N m
kg/m³
N

questions.prompt: A box weighing 60 N rests on the floor. The area in contact is 0.5 m². Calculate the pressure on the floor.
Which statement about pressure in a liquid is correct?
questions.solution: Deeper in a liquid there is more liquid above you pressing down, so the pressure is greater. It acts in every direction, not just down.
options: It decreases with depth
It acts only downwards
It increases with depth
It is the same at every depth

questions.prompt: Calculate the pressure due to the water at a depth of 2 m in a swimming pool. Density of water $= 1000$ kg/m³, $g = 9.8$ N/kg.
The pressure of a gas on a surface is 2000 Pa. The surface has an area of 0.02 m². Calculate the force on the surface.
A chair leg has a square end of area 25 cm². It presses on the floor with a force of 50 N. Calculate the pressure under the leg, in pascals.
questions.solution: Convert the area first: $25$ cm² $= 25 \div 10\,000 = 0.0025$ m². Then $p = \dfrac{50}{0.0025} = 20\,000$ Pa. Leaving the area in cm² gives 2 Pa, which is wrong by a factor of ten thousand.

questions.prompt: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease as you climb a mountain?
questions.solution: Atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight of the air above pressing down. Higher up there is less air above you, and it is less dense, so the pressure is lower. Gravity barely changes over a mountain's height.

markScheme.description: less air above, so less weight pressing down

options: The air molecules move more slowly
There is less air above you, so its weight presses down less
The air above you becomes heavier
Gravity is much weaker at the top

questions.prompt: At what depth in fresh water is the pressure due to the water 49 000 Pa? Density of water $= 1000$ kg/m³, $g = 9.8$ N/kg.
questions.solution: Rearrange $p = h \rho g$ to $h = \dfrac{p}{\rho g} = \dfrac{49\,000}{1000 \times 9.8} = \dfrac{49\,000}{9800} = 5$ m.

questions.prompt: Sea water has a density of 1030 kg/m³. Calculate the pressure due to the sea water at a depth of 10 m. $g = 9.8$ N/kg.
questions.solution: $p = h \rho g = 10 \times 1030 \times 9.8 = 100\,940$ Pa, about 101 kPa: ten metres of sea water adds roughly one atmosphere.

questions.prompt: Atmospheric pressure at the surface of a lake is 101 000 Pa. Calculate the total pressure on a diver at a depth of 15 m. Density of water $= 1000$ kg/m³, $g = 9.8$ N/kg.
questions.solution: The water adds $h \rho g = 15 \times 1000 \times 9.8 = 147\,000$ Pa on top of the atmosphere already pressing on the surface. Total $= 101\,000 + 147\,000 = 248\,000$ Pa. Forgetting the atmosphere loses the last mark.

questions.prompt: A cube of side 0.1 m is fully submerged in water with its top face 0.2 m below the surface. Calculate the upthrust on the cube. Density of water $= 1000$ kg/m³, $g = 9.8$ N/kg.
questions.solution: Pressure on the top face: $0.2 \times 1000 \times 9.8 = 1960$ Pa. The bottom face is at $0.3$ m: $0.3 \times 1000 \times 9.8 = 2940$ Pa. The difference, $980$ Pa, acts on a face of area $0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.01$ m²: $F = 980 \times 0.01 = 9.8$ N upwards. Check: the cube displaces $0.001$ m³ of water, which weighs $0.001 \times 1000 \times 9.8 = 9.8$ N. Upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced.

markScheme.description: pressure at the top, 1960 Pa, and at the bottom, 2940 Pa

questions.prompt: A metal block weighs 12 N. When it is fully submerged in water the upthrust on it is 9.8 N. Calculate the resultant force on the block.
questions.solution: Weight acts down, upthrust acts up. Resultant $= 12 - 9.8 = 2.2$ N downwards, so the block sinks. It would float only if the upthrust could reach its weight.

markScheme.description: weight and upthrust identified as opposite

questions.prompt: A diver descends from 5 m to 25 m in sea water of density 1030 kg/m³. Calculate the increase in pressure on the diver. $g = 9.8$ N/kg.
questions.solution: Only the change in depth matters: $\Delta h = 25 - 5 = 20$ m. $\Delta p = \Delta h \, \rho g = 20 \times 1030 \times 9.8 = 201\,880$ Pa. Atmospheric pressure is the same at both depths, so it cancels.

questions.prompt: An elephant weighs 40 000 N and stands on four feet, each of area 0.05 m². A person weighs 600 N and stands on two stiletto heels, each of area 0.0001 m². How many times greater is the pressure under the heels than under the elephant's feet?
questions.solution: Elephant: total area $4 \times 0.05 = 0.2$ m², so $p = 40\,000 \div 0.2 = 200\,000$ Pa. Heels: total area $2 \times 0.0001 = 0.0002$ m², so $p = 600 \div 0.0002 = 3\,000\,000$ Pa. Ratio $= 3\,000\,000 \div 200\,000 = 15$. The much smaller force wins because the area is smaller by far more.

questions.prompt: Explain why the pressure in a liquid increases with depth, and why a fully submerged object experiences an upward force.
questions.skill: six-mark explanation of pressure and upthrust
questions.solution: Level-marked. Level 3 links the weight of the liquid above to pressure, states that pressure acts in all directions, and derives upthrust from the pressure at the bottom face being greater than at the top face.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account with some links between points
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete account with every step linked and correct physics terms

criteria.text: Pressure in a liquid is caused by the weight of the liquid above pressing down on the liquid below
Deeper down there is more liquid above, so a greater weight and a greater pressure: $p = h \rho g$
Pressure in a fluid acts in every direction, at right angles to any surface
The bottom face of a submerged object is deeper than the top face, so the pressure on it is greater
Greater pressure on the same area means a greater force on the bottom face than on the top face
The difference between those two forces is a resultant force upwards, the upthrust, equal to the weight of liquid displaced

questions.modelAnswer: The pressure at a point in a liquid is caused by the weight of the liquid above it. Going deeper means more liquid above, so a greater weight pressing down and a greater pressure, which is why $p = h \rho g$ grows with $h$. That pressure acts in all directions, at right angles to any surface it meets. For an object under the surface, the bottom face is deeper than the top face, so the pressure on the bottom is greater. Pressure times area is force, and the faces have the same area, so the force pushing up on the bottom is larger than the force pushing down on the top. The difference is a resultant force upwards, called upthrust, and it equals the weight of the liquid the object has pushed aside.

questions.prompt: Describe a simple model of the Earth's atmosphere and use it to explain why atmospheric pressure decreases with height above the surface.
questions.solution: The model: a thin layer of air, held to the Earth by gravity, that becomes less dense the higher you go. Pressure at any height is caused by the weight of the air above. Higher up there is less air above and it is less dense, so its weight is less and the pressure is lower.

markScheme.description: atmosphere as a thin layer of air around the Earth, held by gravity
air becomes less dense with height
atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight of the air above pressing down
higher up there is less air above, so less weight and less pressure

criteria.text: The atmosphere is a thin layer of air around the Earth, held there by gravity
The air gets less dense with height, because gas molecules are pulled towards the surface and the air can be compressed
Atmospheric pressure is caused by air molecules colliding with surfaces, which in total is the weight of the air above pressing down
At greater height there is less air above, and it is thinner, so less weight presses down and the pressure is lower

questions.modelAnswer: The atmosphere is a thin layer of air around the Earth, held to it by gravity. The air is densest at the surface and gets less dense with height, because the gas can be compressed and the molecules are pulled downwards. Atmospheric pressure at any level is caused by air molecules colliding with surfaces, and in total that is the weight of all the air above that level. Higher up there is less air above you, and what there is, is less dense, so its weight is smaller and the pressure is lower.

questions.prompt: A boat of mass 500 kg floats on fresh water. Calculate the volume of water it displaces. Density of water $= 1000$ kg/m³, $g = 9.8$ N/kg.
questions.solution: Floating means the upthrust equals the weight. Weight $= 500 \times 9.8 = 4900$ N, so the upthrust is 4900 N, which is the weight of the water displaced. Mass of water displaced $= 4900 \div 9.8 = 500$ kg, and its volume $= 500 \div 1000 = 0.5$ m³. A floating object always displaces its own mass of water.

markScheme.description: weight $= 500 \times 9.8 = 4900$ N, so 500 kg of water displaced

examTechnique.body:
Pressure questions are short and the marks are lost to units, not physics. Areas arrive in cm² and have to become m²; the answer to $p = F/A$ is in Pa and the question may want kPa. $p = F/A$ has to be recalled; $p = h \rho g$ is on the sheet. Then read the wording: *pressure due to the water* is $h \rho g$ alone, *total pressure* adds the atmosphere, *increase in pressure* is $\Delta h \, \rho g$ with the atmosphere cancelling.

The six-mark explanations follow a fixed chain. For depth: weight of liquid above, more liquid deeper, more pressure. For upthrust: bottom face deeper, greater pressure, greater force, resultant upwards. For the atmosphere: thin layer, less dense with height, pressure is the weight of air above. Give every link.
examinerErrors: Dividing a force by an area in cm² and giving the answer in Pa. Convert to m² first: $1$ m² $= 10\,000$ cm².
Hunting for $p = F/A$ on the equation sheet. It is not there.
Forgetting atmospheric pressure when the question asks for the *total* pressure at a depth, or adding it when the question asks only for the pressure *due to the water*.
Saying pressure in a liquid acts *downwards*. It acts in every direction, at right angles to any surface.
Explaining upthrust as *water pushing up* with no reason. The mark is for the bottom face being deeper, so at higher pressure, so with a larger force than the top face.
Explaining atmospheric pressure falling with height by *weaker gravity*. Gravity barely changes; the reason is less air above, and thinner air.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer converts every area to m² in the first line and states which pressure the question wants, total or due to the liquid, before calculating. It can derive $p = h \rho g$ from the weight of a column, and it calculates upthrust as the pressure difference between two faces times their area, then checks it against the weight of displaced fluid. Its explanations run as a chain with no missing link: more liquid above, more weight, more pressure; deeper face, more pressure, more force, resultant up; thin layer, thinner with height, less air above, less pressure.
